What Is High Blood Pressure?

High Blood Pressure and Diabetes · Lesson 3

What Is High Blood Pressure?

A flipchart for Care Group meetings. Show the picture side to the group. Turn to the text side to read the story, the questions and the messages.

  • Next and Back, or a swipe, turn the page.
  • Tap a picture to make it fill the screen.
  • Text shows what the facilitator reads. Picture goes back.

Lesson 3 at a glance

90 minutes. Bring the attendance registers and this flipchart. The Activity Leader brings three sealed sachets of drinking water, a pin or needle, and a basin.

Before the pictures

Game: Pass the Squeeze. Everyone holds hands in a circle. Squeeze the hand of the person on your right. The squeeze passes round the circle. Send it faster, then send one each way.

Recall Lesson 2. Ask the group to name the Four Helpers and show the four hand signs.

Commitments. Ask: “What was your commitment at the last lesson? Have you been able to keep it?”

After the pictures

The Water Sachet. Hold a water sachet over the basin and prick one small hole. Say: “This sachet is like a blood vessel. The water is like the blood.”

  • Squeeze gently: a soft stream. “This is like normal blood pressure.”
  • Squeeze hard: the water shoots out and the sachet stretches. “This is like high blood pressure.”
  • Ask: “What will happen to this sachet if I squeeze it hard all day, every day?” It grows weak. It may burst. “In the brain, a blood vessel can block or burst. That is a stroke.”
  • Let two participants try. Ask one to hold a sachet with closed eyes while another squeezes. “Could the sachet tell us how hard it was squeezed? The body also does not tell us. The cuff tells us.”
  • Call out “brain”, “eyes”, “heart” and “kidneys”. Participants touch the head, the eyes, the chest and the lower back.

Discuss barriers. Ask: “Is there anything that might prevent you from going for your checks and taking care of your blood pressure when you feel well?”

Request commitments. Ask: “Based on what you have heard today, what commitment will you make?” Each person chooses. Do not press anyone who is not ready.

Picture 3.1Story: Naa Visits Mr. Mensah

Picture 3.1 · text sideStory: Naa Visits Mr. Mensah

Read the story aloud.

Auntie Naa has taken her medicine for one week. She feels the same as before. She asks herself, “Is this medicine doing anything?”

She goes to visit her neighbour, Mr. Mensah. He says, “For many years the nurses told me my BP was high. But I felt nothing. I was strong. I drove my taxi every day. So I stopped going to the clinic.”

His wife, Auntie Esi, says, “Then one morning he could not lift his arm. We did not know that the pressure was working quietly inside him.”

Naa walks home slowly. She asks herself, “What is this pressure? What is it doing inside me?”

Ask the group.

  • Why did Mr. Mensah stop going to the clinic?
  • What do people in our community say BP feels like?
  • What do you think high blood pressure does inside the body?

Encourage discussion. Do not correct “wrong” answers. Let everyone give an opinion. This page is for discussion, not for teaching.

Say “Let us compare your ideas with the messages on the following pages.”

Picture 3.2Blood Pushes on the Blood Vessels

Picture 3.2 · text sideBlood Pushes on the Blood Vessels

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

The heart pushes blood through the whole body.

  • The heart pushes blood through tubes called blood vessels. It does this all day and all night.
  • The blood carries food and air to every part of the body.
  • The push of the blood on the walls of the blood vessels is called blood pressure. Everyone has blood pressure.
B

When the push is too strong, day after day, it is called high blood pressure.

  • Some people call it BP or hypertension.
  • Blood pressure goes up and down during the day. In high blood pressure, it stays too high.
C

You cannot feel your blood pressure. Only the cuff can tell.

  • Most people with high blood pressure feel nothing.
  • A headache or a hot body does not tell you your pressure. A person can have a headache with normal pressure, and no headache with high pressure.

Ask the group.

  • Have you ever felt well on a day when the nurse said your pressure was high?
  • What will you say to a person who says, “I know when my BP is up”?
Additional information for the facilitator

How it is found. A health worker finds high blood pressure by measuring it on two different days. Lesson 5 explains the two numbers. Do not teach numbers today.

“I can feel my BP.” Many people in Ghana say this. Do not argue. Say that the feelings are real, but they are not a measure. The cuff is the only measure.

Very high blood pressure. When blood pressure is very high, a person may have a severe headache, chest pain, dizziness or difficulty breathing. A person with these signs should go to the health facility at once. Lesson 24 covers emergencies.

Picture 3.3High Pressure Slowly Harms the Body

Picture 3.3 · text sideHigh Pressure Slowly Harms the Body

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

Year after year, high pressure harms the brain, the eyes, the heart and the kidneys.

  • The strong push damages the blood vessels. They become stiff and narrow. Some become weak.
  • The harm comes slowly and quietly, over many years.
B

It can cause a stroke or a weak heart. It can make the kidneys fail and the sight grow weak.

  • In the brain, a blood vessel can block or burst. This is a stroke.
  • The heart works too hard and becomes weak. The person is short of breath and the feet swell.
  • The kidneys can stop cleaning the blood. The eyes can lose sight.
C

When you control your blood pressure, you protect your body.

  • The Four Helpers bring the pressure down and keep it down.
  • It is never too late to start.

Ask the group.

  • Do you know someone who has had a stroke? What happened?
  • Naa asked, “Is this medicine doing anything?” What can we tell her now?
Additional information for the facilitator

Sources. The World Health Organization states that most people with high blood pressure feel no symptoms, and that high blood pressure can cause heart attack, heart failure, stroke and kidney damage. It can also damage the blood vessels at the back of the eye.

Do not frighten. The purpose of this page is to explain why a person who feels well still needs care. Spend more time on the third picture than on the second.

People who have had a stroke. Someone in the group may have had a stroke, or may care for someone who has. Speak with respect. Controlling blood pressure after a stroke lowers the chance of a second one.
